                                                        Abstract
     We show that a version of the generalised information ratio of Lattimore and György (2021) deter-
     mines the asymptotic minimax regret for all finite-action partial monitoring games provided that (a)
     the standard definition of regret is used but the latent space where the adversary plays is potentially
     infinite; or (b) the regret introduced by Rustichini (1999) is used and the latent space is finite. Our
     results are complemented by a number of examples. For any p ∈ [1/2, 1] there exists an infinite par-
     tial monitoring game for which the minimax regret over n rounds is np up to subpolynomial factors
     and there exist finite games for which the minimax Rustichini regret is n4/7 up to subpolynomial
     factors.
     Keywords: Partial monitoring; bandits; information ratio.


1. Introduction
The minimax asymptotic regret for partial monitoring is only understood for finite games and where
the notion of regret compares the learner’s accumulated losses to the loss of the best action in
hindsight. For many partial monitoring games the learner is at a severe disadvantage compared to
the adversary because the signal function may be relatively uninformative. The notion of regret
introduced by Rustichini (1999) serves as a better measure of performance for these games, as it
measures the learner’s performance compared to a baseline that is achievable, while the standard
notion of regret may be linear. Our main contribution is twofold. We show that the generalised
information ratio of Lattimore and György (2021) determines the asymptotic minimax regret for
all finite-action games where either (a) the standard regret is used but the latent space where the
adversary plays is possibly infinite; or (b) the definition of the regret proposed by Rustichini (1999)
is used and the latent space is finite. To state our main theorem informally, for λ > 1 let

Related work Partial monitoring and the non-standard definition of the regret used in part of
this work was proposed by Rustichini (1999), who proved a Hannan-type consistency result using
an argument based on Blackwell approachability (Blackwell, 1956). More recent work on partial
monitoring has focussed on finite games using the classical definition of the regret, where the learner
competes with the best action in hindsight. A long line of work covering various cases (Piccolboni
and Schindelhauer, 2001; Cesa-Bianchi et al., 2006; Foster and Rakhlin, 2012; Antos et al., 2013;
Lattimore and Szepesvári, 2019a) led to a complete classification of finite partial monitoring games
(Bartók et al., 2014). This shows that the minimax regret for all such games is either 0, Θ(n1/2 ),
Θ(n2/3 ) or Θ(n), with the leading constants and rate depending on the structure of the game. More
recent work has developed simple algorithms and improved dependence on constants (Lattimore
and Szepesvári, 2019b, 2020). As far as we know, there has been no general study of infinite partial
monitoring games, though of course many specific instances fall into this category (bandits with a
continuum of possible losses, for example).
    Besides Rustichini (1999), few authors have directly considered partial monitoring with Rusti-
chini’s regret. Lugosi et al. (2008) improve on the results of Rustichini (1999) by providing rates
and high probability bounds, which in the general case are O(n4/5 ) with certain special cases giving
improved bounds. The setting can be viewed as an instance of the even more general problem of
Blackwell approachability with partial monitoring studied by Perchet (2011b); Mannor and Shamir
(2011); Mannor et al. (2014) and Kwon and Perchet (2017). When applied to our setting, the

     Our approach for proving upper bounds is based on the duality between information directed
sampling (Russo and Van Roy, 2014) and its connection to quantities involved in bounding the regret
of mirror descent (Zimmert and Lattimore, 2019; Lattimore and György, 2021). The principle
novelty here is new lower bounds in terms of the information ratio. While one might guess that
the relative entropy might be the notion of information gain most suitable for this, it turns out that
defining the information gain as an expected Bregman divergence between a posterior and prior with
respect to the logarithmic barrier (rather than negentropy) is easier to work with. Correspondingly,
our algorithm is based on mirror descent with the logarithmic barrier as a potential function.
     A recent paper by Foster et al. (2021) investigates a related idea and also prove upper and lower
bounds in terms of an information-ratio-like quantity. Their results are stronger in some dimensions
and weaker in others. For example, while we consider adversarial partial monitoring problems,
they focus on stochastic problems with bandit feedback (but can handle contextual problems). On
the other hand, our work essentially relies on a (small) finite action set and only characterises the
minimax regret in terms of the horizon, while their methods are suitable for large action sets and
yield bounds that demonstrate dependencies on other game-dependent quantities. One might hope
to one day get the best of all these worlds, though at the moment it seems some real new idea is
needed for such a result.

Computation complexity The computation complexity of Algorithm 1 depends on the structure
of the game. For finite Z, there are two challenges. First, some pre-computation is needed to find
Vm . The optimisation to find πt and v̂t is a convex program and can also be solved to reasonable
precision in polynomial time. Updating qt is naively a convex program as well, but can be solved
analytically except for a line search. The optimal tuning of η given in Eq. (4) is probably hard to find
but there is no problem tuning the learning rate online as explained by Lattimore and György (2021).
All up, for medium-sized Rustichini games Algorithm 1 is a reasonably practical option. For infinite
games the optimisation problem to find πt and v̂t remains convex but is infinite-dimensional. In this
case we view the arguments as more of a tool for understanding the regret and an inspiration for
algorithm design.

4. Cell Structure for Rustichini’s Regret
Before the proof of Lemma 6 for the Rustichini setting we need to explore the combinatorial and
geometric structure of Rustichini’s regret. These concepts are needed anyway to understand why
Rustichini games do not admit the same classification as finite partial monitoring games and to
understand our example in Section 5. Assume for this section that we are in the Rustichini setting
so that V and V? are defined as in Eq. (2) and Z is finite and K is the probability simplex over Z.
    The idea is to appropriately generalise the cell decomposition used in the standard finite setting,
which was introduced by Piccolboni and Schindelhauer (2001) and played a fundamental role in all
subsequent work. A morally similar structure is used by Kwon and Perchet (2017), but the setting
is different and matching the ideas does not seem straightforward. The most important takeaway is
that policies can be optimal on multiple cells, which is not true in the standard setting.
    Recall that V? (x) = minα∈[m] Vm (x)α with Vm : K → Rm linear. For α ∈ [m], the cell of
α is the convex polytope Pα = {x ∈ K : V? (x) = Vm (x)α }. The set F = ∪α∈[m] faces(Pα ) is a
polyhedral complex (see Appendix A) and corresponds to the cell decomposition in standard finite
partial monitoring games. A policy π ∈ ∆k is optimal at x ∈ K if ∆(π, x) = 0 and the set of
such policies is denoted by N(x) = {π ∈ ∆k : ∆(π, x) = 0}. Note that N(x) is nonempty by
the definition of ∆. The following lemma shows that N(x) only depends on the face F such that
x ∈ ri(F ). The proof is given in Appendix B.

Lemma 8 Suppose that F ∈ F and x, y ∈ ri(F ). Then N(x) = N(y).

    Based on Lemma 8, it makes sense to define N(F ) = N(x) where x ∈ ri(F ) is any point in the
relative interior of F . Note that because x 7→ ∆(π, x) is continuous, it follows immediately that
∆(π, x) = 0 for all x ∈ F and π ∈ N(F ). Continuity of ∆ also implies that N(F ) is closed for all
faces F ∈ F. Further, π 7→ ∆(π, x) is convex and piecewise linear for any x, so N(F ) is a convex
polytope. An essential difference between the cell decomposition in the standard setting and the
Rustichini setting is that N(Pα ) and N(Pβ ) are not necessary disjoint for distinct α, β ∈ [m]. The
importance of this difference will become apparent in the next section.

partial monitoring shows that λ? ≥ 2 and since the unrestricted game is certainly not easier it

Infinite action sets Our analysis heavily relies on the action set being finite. One roundabout
demonstration that the ideas cannot be generalised to infinite action sets without heavy modification
is that for infinite action sets the adversarial and stochastic regret are no longer the same (Cesa-
Bianchi et al., 2021, for example).
Other questions At the moment we do not know how to obtain high probability bounds in terms
of the information ratio, which would be at least one route towards handling non-oblivious adver-
saries. Our analysis shows that the minimax information ratio with respect to the logarithmic barrier
characterises the regret. An interesting question is whether or not the same result holds when the
logarithmic barrier is replaced by the negentropy, when the information gain would correspond to
the usual mutual information. The obstruction in our current analysis is essentially Eq. (5), which
does not hold anymore. Even if the minimax information ratio with the negentropy does not yield
a classification theorem, some version of exponential weights may still have good results. Devraj
et al. (2021) hints that this may sometimes be possible. Understanding this may be important be-
cause the logarithmic barrier has a serious limitation that the diameter of its potential is linear in the
dimension, which makes it poorly suited for high-dimensional structured problems.

Appendix F. Comparing the notions of regret
There is a subtle connection between the Rustichini and the standard regret. By Theorem 3, the
minimax asymptotic regret for both settings is determined by the minimax information ratio and the
resulting value of λ? . Given a game G = (L, S), let λs? (G) be the value of λ? in game G when the
standard regret is used and λr? (G) be its value when the Rustichini regret is used. Throughout this
section, assume that Z is finite and let V and V? be the Rustichini versions as defined in Eq. (2).
     By our main theorem and the upper bounds by (Kwon and Perchet, 2017) we know that λr? (G) ≤
3 for all finite games. The classification theorem for finite partial monitoring (Bartók et al., 2014)
and our Theorem 3 show that λs? (G) ∈ {1, 2, 3, ∞}. Games with λs? (G) = ∞ are called hopeless
and the learner suffers linear minimax standard regret. So the Rustichini and standard regret are
not the same on these games. An example is the game in Section 5, for which λs? (G) = ∞ and
λr? (G) = 7/3. A natural question is whether or not λs? (G) = λr? (G) when λs? (G) ∈ {1, 2, 3}. The
answer is obviously yes for all games where xRy if and only if x = y. The answer also turns out
to be yes for the large class of non-degenerate games. For degenerate games there can be subtle
differences.
